blocks.text: Put a helper next to a client to handle its outbound calls to a remote resource, so the client stays simple.

The client talks to a local endpoint as if the resource were next door. The **ambassador** owns the awkward parts of reaching the real one: service discovery, sharding, connection pooling, TLS, retries and failover. It is a sidecar specialized for the outbound path.

items: **Client sees:** one stable local address and a simple protocol.
**Useful for:** legacy clients you cannot modify.

blocks.text: Think of it as the client's diplomat: it speaks the remote system's language and policies so the client doesn't have to.

walkthrough.note: The client-side contract is a plain `KeyValue`. Whether it is a map, one server or a cluster is invisible to callers.
A scripted fake node: it records every attempt in a shared trace and fails deterministically when `up` is false, so failover is testable without real time.
The ambassador picks the shard from a stable hash of the key, then tries that shard's replicas in order. Only if all fail does the client see an error.
The application code is a single call. It has no shard map, no retry loop and no knowledge of replicas.
Two shards of two replicas. Replica `a1` is down. Calls to shard A fall through to `a2` while shard B answers on its first replica.

blocks.text: A legacy app talking to a sharded Redis cluster.

An old billing service only speaks to one Redis address and has no cluster awareness. Rewriting its client library is out of scope. Next to each instance runs a proxy that exposes `localhost:6379`, hashes keys to shards, follows failover to replicas and reuses pooled connections. The app is unchanged while the cache tier grows from two shards to eight.

lists.title: Use when
items: A client cannot be changed but must reach a complex remote resource.
Connection policy (retry, TLS, discovery) should be shared across clients and languages.
You want to test the client against a local stub.

lists.title: Avoid when
items: One client library already does the job and you control the code.
Added localhost latency or another moving part outweighs the benefit.

lists.title: Pitfalls
items: Blind retries through the ambassador on non-idempotent calls cause duplicates.
Hidden failover can mask an outage; export metrics from the ambassador.
Client timeouts must exceed the ambassador's retry budget, or they cancel mid-failover.

lists.title: Overuse smells
items: An ambassador that transforms business data instead of managing connectivity.
One ambassador per call site instead of per client instance.

lists.title: Modern Java
items: Sealed result types or checked exceptions model 'all replicas down' explicitly for callers.
For new code, a client library with the same policy may beat a separate process.

rows.difference: An ambassador is a sidecar dedicated to one concern: the client's outbound access to a remote resource. A sidecar is the general co-located helper.
Same stand-in shape, but an ambassador is deployed beside the client and adds connection policy; a remote proxy simply represents one remote object.
An adapter converts one interface into another in-process. An ambassador keeps the interface and manages how the remote call is made.
Breakers, retries and timeouts live naturally in the ambassador so clients inherit them.
The ambassador is a good place for retry with backoff and failover, applied uniformly to every client.

modelAnswer.text: An ambassador is a helper beside the client that makes outbound calls to a remote resource: it hides discovery, sharding, TLS, retries and failover behind a simple local address. It is a sidecar specialized for outbound access, and useful when the client cannot be changed.

keyPoints: Helper deployed with the client for its outbound calls
Client sees a simple local address
Owns sharding, retries, failover, TLS and credentials
A sidecar specialized for the outbound path
Lets unchanged legacy clients reach modern resources
